q: On sunscreen labels, what does the abbreviation SPF stand for?
note: It compares the UV dose needed to redden protected skin with that for unprotected skin.

q: The SPF number on a sunscreen mainly measures protection against which type of UV rays?
note: These shorter-wavelength rays are the main cause of sunburn.

q: The PA+ to PA++++ rating on sunscreens grades protection against which type of UV?
note: The rating system was introduced in Japan in 1996.

q: Which type of UV rays largely passes through ordinary window glass?
note: Ordinary glass blocks most of the shorter UV wavelengths but lets much of the longer ones through.

q: Which band of UV radiation is almost completely absorbed by Earth's atmosphere before reaching the ground?
note: Its germ-killing power is used in lamps that disinfect water and surfaces.

q: Applied as tested, an SPF 30 sunscreen filters out roughly what share of UVB rays?
note: SPF 50 filters about 98%, so higher numbers add only small gains.

q: Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide and which other white mineral as UV filters?
note: Very fine particles make modern versions look far less white on skin.

q: Myth-buster: according to dermatologists, can dark skin be damaged by the sun's UV rays?
a: Yes, it can still be damaged
options: Yes, it can still be damaged
note: The American Academy of Dermatology says people of every skin colour can get skin cancer.

q: Myth-buster: regrowing shaved hair feels coarse because the razor leaves each hair with what kind of tip?
note: Shaving does not change a hair's thickness, colour or rate of growth.

q: Healthy human skin is naturally slightly acidic on its surface, with a pH of roughly what?
note: Neutral pure water sits at 7, so skin is mildly acidic by comparison.

q: What is the name for the thin, slightly acidic protective film on the skin's surface?
note: Its acidity helps keep harmful organisms in check.

q: Which pigment-making cells in the skin's deepest outer layer give skin, hair and eyes their colour?
note: They pass their pigment in tiny packets to neighbouring skin cells.

q: Which protein, the most abundant in the human body, gives skin its firmness and strength?
note: It is also a major part of tendons, bones and cartilage.

q: Which stretchy protein lets skin spring back into shape after it is pulled or pinched?
What is the oily, waxy substance that glands attached to hair follicles release onto the skin?
note: It helps waterproof skin and hair.

q: What is the Latin name of the tough outermost skin layer, made of flattened dead cells?
Roughly how long do new skin cells take to rise through the outer skin layer and flake off?
note: The renewal process slows down with age.

q: Goosebumps appear when tiny muscles attached to hair follicles contract. What are these muscles called?
note: In furry animals, the same reflex fluffs up the fur for warmth.

q: Myth-buster: what actually makes the tip of a blackhead look dark?
note: The pore stays open, so the plug inside darkens where it meets the air.

q: A 'non-comedogenic' label claims a skincare product is formulated not to cause what?
note: A comedo is the medical name for a blocked pore, such as a whitehead.

q: A 'hypoallergenic' label claims a cosmetic is less likely to cause what?
note: In the US, no federal standard defines when the term can be used.

q: Fresh sweat is nearly odourless. What breaks it down on the skin, creating an unpleasant whiff?
Which glands, found mainly in the armpits, release a thicker, milkier kind of sweat?
Which glands, found almost all over the body, release watery sweat mainly to cool us down?
Antiperspirants reduce sweat by temporarily plugging sweat ducts with salts of which metal?
What is the part of a hair that sits visible above the skin called?
Which outermost layer of a hair strand is made of overlapping scales, like roof tiles?
note: When these scales lie flat, hair reflects more light and looks shinier.

q: What is the active growth phase of a hair follicle called?
note: On the scalp it can last several years, which is why head hair grows so long.

q: On average, roughly how much does scalp hair grow in a month?
According to the American Academy of Dermatology, how many scalp hairs does a person normally shed a day?
Dandruff is strongly linked to which genus of yeast that feeds on scalp oils?
note: It lives on most people's skin; some scalps simply react to it more.

q: Perms and chemical straighteners reshape hair by breaking which strong chemical bonds inside it?
note: Wetting and blow-drying only break weaker bonds, so those styles don't last.

q: Many permanent hair dyes contain which pungent alkaline chemical to swell hair open so colour can enter?
note: Ammonia-free dyes usually use a milder alkali such as ethanolamine.

q: 'Black henna' skin designs can cause severe skin reactions because of which added dye chemical, known by three letters?
note: The same chemical is found in many permanent dark hair dyes.

q: What is the name of the orange-red dye molecule in henna leaves?
note: It binds to proteins in the outer skin, so the stain fades as that skin sheds.

q: Why does mehndi usually stain the palms and soles darker than other areas?
a: Their outer skin layer is thicker
options: Their outer skin layer is thicker

q: Which reddish-yellow natural hair pigment resists lightening, often leaving brassy orange tones?
note: Bleach breaks down hair's darker brown-black pigment more easily.

q: Natural red hair is most closely associated with variants of which gene?
note: It influences which type of pigment hair follicles mostly produce.

q: What is the scientific name for split ends in hair?
note: Split strands can't be permanently fused back together.

q: Minoxidil, now used in hair regrowth products, was originally developed as a tablet for which condition?
note: Unexpected hair growth in patients led to its use on the scalp.

q: Pattern hair loss is linked to follicles' sensitivity to which hormone, abbreviated DHT?
note: It is made from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase.

q: Coconut oil can soak into hair, unlike mineral oil, mainly because of which fatty acid?
What is the pale half-moon shape at the base of a fingernail called?
note: Its name comes from the Latin for 'little moon'.

q: Myth-buster: small white spots on fingernails are most often caused by what?
note: The medical name for the spots is leukonychia.

q: Ordinary nail polish dries and hardens mainly through which process?
note: Gel polish is different and needs a lamp to set.

q: Gel nail polish hardens under a UV or LED lamp through which chemical process?
note: The lamp triggers small molecules to link up into long chains.

q: Why doesn't permanent hair dye simply wash out?
a: Colour molecules form inside the hair
options: It glues onto the hair surface
It is sealed in by conditioner
Colour molecules form inside the hair
Hair cleansers can't reach dyed hair
note: Small colourless ingredients enter the hair and react there to form large coloured molecules.

q: Which strong-smelling solvent is the classic ingredient in nail polish remover?
note: Removers without it often use ethyl acetate instead.

q: Glycerin and hyaluronic acid are both which type of moisturising ingredient, one that draws water into skin?
Petroleum jelly is a classic example of which type of moisturiser, forming a seal that stops water escaping?
Which type of moisturising ingredient softens and smooths skin by filling the gaps between skin cells?
note: The word comes from the Latin for 'to soften'.

q: Retinol, a common skincare ingredient, is a form of which vitamin?
note: Its prescription-strength relative, tretinoin, is also called retinoic acid.

q: Salicylic acid belongs to which class of exfoliating acids, known by three letters?
Glycolic acid belongs to which class of exfoliating acids, known by three letters?
Why can salicylic acid work deeper inside oily pores than glycolic acid?
Glycolic acid, a popular exfoliant, occurs naturally in which crop?
On cosmetic ingredient lists, vitamin E usually appears under which chemical name?
note: As an antioxidant, it also helps stop oils in a product turning rancid.

q: Which waxy lipids make up roughly half, by weight, of the fats in the skin's protective barrier?
Squalane in skincare is made from squalene, first isolated from the oil of which sea predator?
note: Most cosmetic squalane today is plant-derived instead.

q: Parabens are added to many cosmetics as which kind of ingredient?
note: They stop moulds and other organisms growing once a product has been opened.

q: Lanolin, a waxy ingredient in lip balms and creams, is obtained from the fleece of which animal?
note: On the animal, it helps waterproof the coat.

q: Shea butter comes from the nuts of a tree native to which continent?
Which shiny, flaky mineral gives many eyeshadows and highlighters their shimmer?
Guanine, used for a pearly shimmer in some nail polishes, was traditionally obtained from what?
What type of ingredient keeps oil and water blended together in a cream or lotion?
What class of 'surface-active' molecules lifts oil off hair and skin so water can rinse it away?
In cleansers, the foaming ingredient SLS stands for sodium lauryl what?
Conditioners use positively charged ingredients because damaged hair carries which electrical charge?
note: Opposite charges attract, so conditioning ingredients cling to the hair and reduce frizz.

q: In a perfume, what are the first, lightest scents you notice, fading within minutes, called?
note: Citrus oils are classic examples because they evaporate quickly.

q: What are a perfume's heaviest, longest-lasting scents, which linger for hours, called?
note: Woods, resins and vanilla often play this role.

q: The layer of a perfume that emerges once the opening scents fade is called the what notes?
note: Floral scents often sit in this layer.

q: Which of these fragrance types usually contains the highest concentration of perfume oils?
note: Higher oil concentration generally means the scent lasts longer on skin.

q: Natural musk, once prized in perfumery, came from a gland of which male Himalayan animal?
note: Nearly all musk used in perfumery today is synthetic.

q: Oud, or agarwood, forms when Aquilaria trees produce dark fragrant resin in response to what?
Khus, used in cooling curtains and perfume oils, comes from which part of the vetiver plant?
note: Wetting khus mats releases their earthy scent as the water evaporates.

q: Expert perfumers in the fragrance industry are nicknamed after which body part?
Which country's Rose Valley, near the town of Kazanlak, is famous for producing rose oil?
Coumarin, a compound used in many perfumes, smells like tonka beans and freshly cut what?
In perfume-making, what is the main job of a fixative?
The fougere fragrance family takes its name from the French word for which plant?
note: Ferns have little scent; the name describes an imagined green, herbal accord.

q: The chypre fragrance family is named after the French word for which Mediterranean island?
Enfleurage, an old way of capturing the scent of delicate flowers like tuberose, uses what to absorb it?
note: Fresh petals were pressed onto the layer and replaced repeatedly until it was heavily scented.

q: What is the term for gradually no longer noticing a constant scent, such as your own perfume?
What French perfumery term describes the scent trail a fragrance leaves in the air behind the wearer?
note: The word originally means the wake left behind a boat.

q: Castoreum, historically used in leathery perfumes, comes from which animal?
Neroli oil is distilled from the blossoms of which tree?
Mogra, prized in Indian perfumery and woven into gajras, is a species of which flower?
The Damask rose, a key source of rose oil, is named after which city?
What is multani mitti, the clay used in face packs, called in English?
note: The English name comes from 'fullers', cloth workers who used this clay to clean fabric.

q: Besan, used in traditional ubtan skin pastes, is a flour ground from which pulse?
Kajal is closely related to which ancient eyeliner, also known as surma in parts of India?
note: Homemade kajal is traditionally made from lamp soot mixed with oil.

q: The US FDA warns that traditional surma can contain galena, an ore of which metal?
note: The FDA says lead compounds sometimes make up over half the weight of such products.

q: Pure henna on its own leaves a stain in which colour range?
note: A stain that turns truly black very quickly usually signals added chemical dyes.

q: To dye hair dark brown or black, henna is often used with powdered leaves of which plant?
Amla, a common ingredient in Indian hair oils, is known in English as the Indian what?
Reetha (soapnut) shells lather in water because they contain natural foaming compounds called what?
Gulab jal, or rose water, is traditionally produced by which process?
note: It is often a by-product of making rose oil.

q: Fitkari, the alum block rubbed on skin after a shave, acts as what kind of agent that tightens tissue?
In which year did India ban the testing of cosmetics on animals?
note: A ban on importing animal-tested cosmetics followed later the same year.

q: Tattoos are long-lasting because the ink is placed in which layer of the skin?
note: The outermost layer constantly sheds, so ink placed there would soon fade.

q: Myth-buster: what happens when you pluck out a single grey hair?
a: One hair regrows from that follicle
options: One hair regrows from that follicle
note: A follicle can't multiply, so plucking doesn't spread grey hair.

q: Myth-buster: why can't hot or cold water truly 'open' or 'close' skin pores?
note: Warmth can soften the oil inside pores, which is where the myth comes from.

q: Chemical UV filters in sunscreen absorb UV rays and release that energy mainly as what?
note: Mineral filters also mostly absorb UV rather than simply reflecting it.

q: In the US, 'water resistant' sunscreens must state protection for either 40 or how many minutes?
note: The FDA's 2011 labelling rules stopped sunscreens being called 'waterproof'.

q: Myth-buster: in dermatology, what does a suntan indicate?
note: Tanning is the skin's defence response to injury to its DNA.

q: Sunless self-tanners darken skin with a simple sugar known by which three-letter abbreviation?
note: It reacts with proteins in dead outer skin cells, so the colour fades as they shed.

q: Tightly curly hair typically grows from hair follicles of which shape?

A lost fingernail typically takes about how long to grow back fully?
note: Toenails are slower, often taking 12 to 18 months.

q: Eyebrow hairs stay short mainly because, compared with scalp hair, their growth phase is what?

What term describes skin ageing caused mainly by long-term sun exposure rather than time?
Tiny scrubbing beads banned from US rinse-off cosmetics by a 2015 law are called what?

q: In which year did the EU's full ban on selling cosmetics tested on animals take effect?
Cosmetic ingredient lists generally name ingredients in which order?
note: Ingredients below 1% can usually be listed in any order at the end.

q: An open-jar symbol marked '12M' on a cosmetic means what?
note: It is known as the period-after-opening symbol.

q: A 2020 Harvard study in mice linked stress-related greying to which part of the nervous system?

Dry hair cleansers soak up excess scalp oil mainly using which kind of absorbent powder?
note: Rice and corn versions of it are common choices.

a: No, growth happens at the follicle
options: Yes, but only for short hair
No, growth happens at the follicle

note: Some newer 'bio-glitters' are plant-based instead.
